title: HTML comments: syntax, use, and limitations
learningObjectives: Write valid single-line and multi-line HTML comments using the correct delimiters.
Explain where comments can appear in an HTML document and how browsers treat them during parsing.
Use comments to record concise implementation context without repeating obvious markup.
Recognize that comments are delivered to the browser and are not a secure place for secrets or private data.
Diagnose malformed comment boundaries and understand why comments should not be used to hide active content.

understand.concept: An HTML comment begins with <!-- and ends with -->. The browser parses the comment as part of the source but does not display its contents as ordinary page text. Comments can help developers leave short notes, mark sections during development, or temporarily exclude a fragment while debugging. They are not a security boundary: comments are usually present in the downloaded document source and can be inspected by anyone who can access the page. HTML comment syntax has parsing restrictions, so avoid placing -- inside comment text and always close the comment correctly. Do not use comments as a substitute for removing unused code or documenting important behaviour in a proper project document.
understand.whyItMatters: Comments can improve collaboration when they explain non-obvious decisions, but malformed or excessive comments make source harder to read. Exposing credentials or personal information in comments creates a security and privacy risk because comments are not hidden from visitors who inspect the source.
understand.analogy: An HTML comment is like a note written in the margin of a document: the reader of the printed page may not see it, but someone examining the original file can.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy understates browser parsing rules. HTML comments are tokens in the document source and are not encrypted, access-controlled, or guaranteed to be removed before delivery.

explain.narrative: Add a concise comment before a complex section, then inspect View Source and the DOM to distinguish source comments from visible page content. Compare a properly closed comment with a malformed one and remove sensitive or stale notes.

examples.code: HomeCourses
examples.explanation: The comment explains the purpose of the following region. It is not displayed as page text, but it remains in the source delivered to the browser.
examples.expectedOutput: A primary navigation region with two links; the comment does not appear as visible text.

examples.code:
Course overview

Explore the available lessons.
examples.explanation: A short TODO can be useful during development, but it must be resolved before release. Do not put passwords, API keys, personal data, or internal secrets in comments.
examples.expectedOutput: A main region with a heading and paragraph; the TODO comment is absent from the rendered page.

practise.guidedTask: Add comments to a sample HTML page to identify two non-obvious sections. Then inspect the page source and confirm that the comments are still visible in the downloaded markup but not rendered as ordinary page text.
practise.independentTask: Review a project for stale TODO notes, malformed comment delimiters, commented-out production code, and accidental secrets. Remove sensitive content and move important implementation documentation into the project's maintained documentation.
hints: Start comments with <!-- and close them with -->.
Avoid -- inside comment text and do not leave comment boundaries open accidentally.
Comments are not private; anyone inspecting the source may read them.

questions.prompt: Which sequence starts an HTML comment?
questions.explanation: HTML comments begin with the less-than sign, exclamation mark, and two hyphens.

questions.prompt: Which sequence closes an HTML comment?
questions.explanation: The closing delimiter is two hyphens followed by a greater-than sign.

questions.prompt: Are HTML comments visible to someone inspecting the downloaded page source?
questions.explanation: Comments are included in the source sent to the browser and can be inspected.

questions.prompt: What is an appropriate use of an HTML comment?
options: Explaining a non-obvious section or temporary development note
questions.answer: Explaining a non-obvious section or temporary development note
questions.explanation: Comments can document intent, but they are not a safe place for secrets.

questions.prompt: Should comments be used to hide unused production code permanently?
options: No, remove unused code or document the decision properly
Yes, comments are a secure archive
Only if the code is JavaScript
questions.answer: No, remove unused code or document the decision properly
questions.explanation: Commented-out code becomes stale and confusing; version control is a better way to preserve history.
